newsitem.title: MOLDOVA: Ex-Soviet Moldova holds free presidential poll.
newsitem.headline: Ex-Soviet Moldova holds free presidential poll.

text.p: Moldovans voted on Sunday in their first multi-party presidential election, hotly contested by three top state officials -- the president, the prime minister and the chairman of parliament.
Less than 100 metres (yards) separate their imposing buildings in the Moldovan capital Chisinau but a tough campaign has driven a deep wedge between the three men who once worked as a team.
President Mircea Snegur, 56, reminds some observers of Russia's Boris Yeltsin. Like the Russian leader in 1993, Snegur is locked in a bitter power struggle with his opponents.
He has led an aggressive and populist campaign. "Give me more power and I will make your life better," is his motto.

Snegur has said that if he won, he would amend the constitution, possible through a referendum, to gain more powers and dissolve the "corrupt" government headed by Andrei Sangheli and the parliament of Petru Lucinschi.
Opponents say Snegur is leading Moldova towards confrontation and inflaming passions the impoverished state can ill afford.
Both Sangheli and Lucinschi told reporters after casting their ballots on Sunday that they would not resign if Snegur won and accused him of acting against the law.

The centre-right Snegur says he wants closer ties with the West and Romania, with which Moldova shares common language and culture. He has forged an alliance with nationalists who want a merger with Romania but says Moldova should stay independent.
Sangheli, 52, soft-spoken and markedly uncharismatic, prides himself for his economic stabilisation programme backed by the International Monetary Fund.
He dismisses nationalists and is leaning towards Russia, Moldova's main energy supplier and biggest market.
His campaign has been based on an image of a man of many deeds and few words -- maybe too few to win a national poll, despite his popularity in some rural areas.
Lucinschi, 56, the intellectual and charismatic former communist leader of Moldova, says he is "just in between the two" and presents himself as a moderate centrist of social- democratic type.
He highlighted his restraint voting early on Sunday. While Snegur and Sangheli told reporters they hoped for a first-round victory, Lucinschi said he would win in the runoff.
Nearly 2,000 polling stations opened at 8 a.m. (0600 GMT) across the ex-Soviet republic of 4.3 million people sandwiched between Romania and Ukraine. Voting lasts 12 hours.
The election law says more than 50 percent of the 2.4 million eligible voters have to take part to make the poll valid but experts expect a much higher turnout.
In the capital Chisinau a steady flow of people headed for the polling stations which, in a Soviet tradition, offered voters well-stocked and cheap buffets.
"I want a better future," said Andrei, a 78-year-old ethnic Russian pensioner. "I want the leaders who work and I do not want the people to live in poverty."
There are six other candidates, including the head of the Communist Party and a radical nationalist.
Experts expect noone of the candidates to win more than 50 percent of the vote in the first round and predict a runoff between the two top contenders for the four year term.
Preliminary results of Sunday's vote are expected on Monday.
The breakaway Dnestr region has banned voting on its territory but voters may cast their ballots outside the area.
The 700,000-strong industrial heartland of Moldova populated mostly by Russians and Ukrainians broke away in 1992 fearing a possible unification between Moldova and Romania.
